instagram.caption: Front Range passenger rail is coming to Longmont by January 2029, with three daily round trips connecting us to Denver Union Station and Fort Collins. And it won't cost taxpayers a dime. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: We've got a date: Front Range passenger rail service will launch by January 2029, with three round trips a day connecting Longmont to Denver Union Station and Fort Collins. The best part? It's already funded through a partnership between CDOT and RTD, so Longmont taxpayers won't pay a cent extra. This week on Unity in the Community, we break down what's coming, how it's paid for, and what it means for getting around the Front Range. What would you use the train for most: commuting to Denver, heading up to Fort Collins, or something else entirely?

bluesky.post: Longmont passenger rail starts January 2029, three round trips daily to Denver Union Station and Fort Collins, at no extra cost to taxpayers. It's happening.

discord.message: New clip up from Unity in the Community: Front Range passenger rail is officially coming to Longmont by January 2029. Three daily round trips to Denver and Fort Collins, already funded through CDOT and RTD, no additional cost to us. Full breakdown in the clip. Curious what y'all think about this one.

instagram.caption: Longmont firefighters are working 96-hour shifts (four days straight) because the department is so understaffed. Calls have increased 86% since 2009, but staffing is only up 13%. Full episode on Unity in the Community, link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Unity in the Community episode, we heard directly from a Longmont firefighter about what the staffing crisis really looks like on the ground. The department is facing 33,000 hours of overtime this year, with some firefighters working mandatory 96-hour shifts, four straight days. Since 2009, emergency calls have jumped 86%, but staffing has only increased by 13%. That gap doesn't just show up in the numbers; it shows up in missed birthdays, exhausted crews, and a fire department stretched thin. What does public safety funding mean to you as a Longmont resident?

bluesky.post: Longmont firefighters are working 96-hour shifts because calls are up 86% since 2009 but staffing is only up 13%. Four days straight.

discord.message: New clip from Unity in the Community is up: Longmont firefighter breaks down the staffing crisis: 33,000 hours of OT this year, some crews working four days straight, and an 86% increase in calls met with only a 13% staffing bump since 2009. Real numbers, real strain. Curious what y'all think about this one. Link's in the usual spot.

instagram.caption: You call 911, the ambulance shows up, and six months later a $2,000 bill lands in your mailbox. On this week's Unity in the Community episode: why Coloradans are still getting hit with surprise ambulance bills, and the legislative fix that got vetoed. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: You call 911. You assume your health insurance will cover the ambulance. Then six months later, a $2,000 bill shows up in the mail. This week on Unity in the Community, we dig into why Coloradans are still getting blindsided by surprise ground ambulance bills, even though many other states have already closed this loophole. The conversation covers a legislative fix that would have solved the problem for public fire department ambulances, and why our governor vetoed it. Have you or someone you know been hit with one of these surprise bills?

bluesky.post: You call 911, assume insurance covers the ambulance, then get a $2,000 bill six months later. Colorado had a chance to fix this and the governor vetoed it.

discord.message: New clip from this week's Unity in the Community episode: the ground ambulance billing problem in Colorado. Surprise $2,000 bills showing up months after a 911 call, a legislative fix that would've closed the loophole, and the veto that kept it broken. Worth a listen if you've ever wondered why healthcare billing in this state is such a mess. Curious what y'all think about this one.

instagram.caption: Downtown Longmont is about to look very different. A five-story, 700-space parking garage is coming to First and Main by 2027, complete with bus rapid transit docks and surrounded by new housing and mixed-use development. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Unity in the Community episode, we dig into one of the biggest infrastructure projects coming to downtown Longmont: a five-story, 700-space parking garage at First and Main, just south of Cheese Importers. It's not just parking, though. The first floor will house 10 bus bays to support regional routes and two new bus rapid transit lines connecting Boulder and Longmont, with housing and mixed-use commercial wrapping the structure. Add in the expanded Coffman Street corridor linking to the Saint Vrain Greenway and Front Range Community College's permanent Boulder County campus nearby, and you're looking at a completely reshaped downtown by 2027. What part of this development are you most curious (or concerned) about?

bluesky.post: Downtown Longmont is getting a 700-space garage by 2027, with bus rapid transit docks on the first floor and mixed-use development all around it. Big changes coming to First and Main.

discord.message: New clip from this week's Unity in the Community episode: breaking down the 700-space parking garage coming to First and Main by 2027. Five stories, 10 bus bays for regional and BRT routes, plus housing and commercial wrapped around it. Also touches on the Coffman Street expansion and Front Range Community College's permanent campus. Curious what y'all think about this one. Lots of infrastructure change packed into a pretty tight timeframe.

instagram.caption: A friend reached into her pocket and handed over a $20 bill, and it became one candidate's favorite donation. Why? Because it proved democracy doesn't have to be funded by the wealthy alone. Hear the full story on this week's Unity in the Community episode, link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Unity in the Community episode, we hear a story that beautifully captures what grassroots democracy can look like. A candidate shares her favorite campaign donation: not the biggest check, but a $20 bill handed over by a friend who doesn't typically give to political campaigns. The friend, a Republican married to a Democrat, had always stayed out of the donation game until one conversation changed her mind. The turning point? Hearing that if regular people don't donate, only the wealthy get to run for office. It's a small moment with a big idea behind it. Have you ever given to a local campaign, and if so, what made you decide to do it?

bluesky.post: A friend who never donates to campaigns reached into her pocket and handed over a $20 bill. Why it became a candidate's favorite donation, on this week's Unity in the Community.

discord.message: New clip from Unity in the Community is up: a candidate tells the story of her favorite campaign donation: a $20 bill from a friend who'd never given to a political campaign before. It's a really vivid moment about why grassroots funding matters and who gets to run for office when only wealthy donors show up. Worth a listen if you're thinking about local democracy stuff. Curious what y'all think about this one.

instagram.caption: Two votes out of three ends the conversation. This week we're unpacking why Boulder County's three-commissioner structure moves so fast, and what gets left behind when it does. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Unity in the Community episode, we dig into the math problem at the heart of Boulder County governance: with three commissioners, two votes means the debate is over. Compare that to Longmont's seven-member city council, where two votes is just the beginning. There's room for a third perspective, a different angle, maybe an idea that doesn't win but still gets heard and considered. It's a structural difference that shapes which voices make it into the decision. What do you think gets lost when the threshold for "done" is that low?

bluesky.post: With three commissioners, two votes ends the conversation. With seven on city council, two votes is just the start. The structure shapes what gets heard.

discord.message: New clip from this week's Unity in the Community episode: a really clear breakdown of the structural problem with Boulder County's three-commissioner setup. Two votes and the debate's over - versus city council's seven members, where there's actually space for a third idea to be heard even if it doesn't win. Curious what y'all think about this one - clips channel or episode page.

instagram.caption: Reliability, affordability, sustainability: balancing all three is how Longmont keeps the lights on when neighboring towns go dark. This week's Unity in the Community breaks down the three-legged stool behind our power policy. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Unity in the Community, we dig into how Longmont balances the three-legged stool of municipal power: reliability, affordability, and sustainability. It's a framework that explains a lot about why our approach looks different from neighboring communities. Case in point: when high winds knocked out power for days across the region, Longmont stayed up and running. The tradeoffs aren't always simple, but the results speak for themselves. What do you value most when it comes to how our city manages power?

bluesky.post: Reliability, affordability, sustainability: the three-legged stool behind Longmont's power. When nearby towns lost electricity for days during windstorms, we kept the lights on.

discord.message: New clip from Unity in the Community (Aug 28): breaking down the three-legged stool of Longmont's power policy (reliability, affordability, sustainability) and why we kept the lights on during those brutal windstorms when neighboring communities went dark for days. Concrete example of how municipal power tradeoffs actually play out. Worth a listen if you've ever wondered why our approach looks different.

instagram.caption: Starting September 27, you can catch an hourly bus from Longmont straight to DIA for just $10. That's not a typo. This week on Unity in the Community, we break down the new direct airport service and what it means for getting out of town (or back home). Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Unity in the Community episode, we learned that Longmont is getting hourly bus service direct to Denver International Airport starting September 27. The fare? Just $10. For seniors, $1.35. This is a huge step for connectivity in Longmont, especially for folks who've been patching together rides or paying for long-term parking every time they fly. The service runs every hour, so whether you're catching an early flight or coming home late, there's a real option now. Have you been waiting for something like this, or are you already planning your first airport trip on the new line?

bluesky.post: Longmont to DIA for $10, hourly service, starting Sept 27. That's a legitimately good deal.

discord.message: New clip up from Unity in the Community: hourly bus service from Longmont to DIA launches September 27 for $10 a ride ($1.35 for seniors). Pretty big news if you've been dealing with airport logistics. Curious what y'all think about this one. Will you use it?
